per_question.question: Who is eligible for the Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)? What requirements does someone have to meet to get in?
per_question.agent_answer:
To be eligible for CAP/DA, a person must be an NC Medicaid beneficiary and must need a nursing-facility level of care, but be able to live safely in the community with waiver supports rather than in an institution. [Policy 3K-2 § 2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2, Community Alternatives Program (CAP)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Basic eligibility for CAP/DA

A person must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program. [Policy 3K-2 § 2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

CAP/DA is a home- and community-based waiver for Medicaid beneficiaries who require institutional care, but whose care can be provided cost-effectively and safely in the community with CAP services. [Policy 3K-2, Community Alternatives Program (CAP)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The policy in effect is the September 1, 2025 amended version, and NC Medicaid’s amendment history says the revision aligned the policy with the renewed CAP/DA waiver approved by CMS. [Policy 3K-2 Change Notice 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## What someone has to meet to get into CAP/DA

NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA only when the beneficiary meets the specific criteria in section 3.2.1. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Those requirements include:

- The person must meet the required HCBS nursing-facility level of care determined by NC Medicaid and require long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- A completed CAP assessment must show a reasonable indication that the person will need at least one CAP/DA waiver service within 30 calendar days of the evaluation. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person must have a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services on a monthly basis to prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Alternatively, the signed service plan may authorize short-term equipment, modification, or technology needed to allow the person to return to or remain in the primary private residence and avoid institutional placement, with the installation completed within three calendar months of service-plan approval. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person must be able to maintain health, safety, and well-being in the primary private residence or another approved location using both formal and informal supports. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Paid care needs must be able to be maintained within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person must have a primary physician who can link and coordinate all medical services. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person must have an emergency back-up and disaster plan identifying who will provide care if direct care staff are unavailable, the primary caregiver has an emergency, or there is a public health emergency. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The emergency and disaster plan is a mandatory requirement that must be completed during service-plan development or within 30 calendar days of initial or annual CAP/DA service-plan approval, and it must be updated quarterly or during an emergency or pandemic. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Level-of-care requirement

The level-of-care determination is for an applicant or current CAP/DA beneficiary who meets a nursing-facility level of care because of a medical diagnosis or physical disability. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

That determination is based on conditions, diagnoses, and treatments showing a need that meets or exceeds Medicaid State Plan nursing-facility level-of-care criteria, plus deficits in activities of daily living that show a need for the waiver’s supportive services. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

A level-of-care determination must be completed at initial enrollment, and an annual level-of-care review is done during the continued-need review assessment. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Medical-necessity overlay

Even when someone fits CAP/DA-specific criteria, services still must be medically necessary, individualized, safe to furnish, and not primarily for convenience. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Waitlist / priority considerations

CAP/DA participation is considered on a first-come, first-served basis, but some applicants move to the top of an existing waitlist if they meet listed priority factors. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Priority categories include, among others, people ages 18 to 20 transitioning from CAP/C, people transitioning from a nursing facility, certain adults identified by DSS/APS as at risk, people with Alzheimer’s disease or a related disorder, adults already in another approved 1915(c) waiver who want to transition to CAP/DA, and beneficiaries in hospice with an expected end date within six months who are at risk of entering a non-hospice institution. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## When someone is not eligible / not covered

CAP/DA is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in section 2.0 or the coverage criteria in section 3.0. [Policy 3K-2 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Consumer-directed CAP/DA

If the person wants consumer-directed services, they must meet all the regular CAP/DA criteria and also complete the required self-assessment and introductory training, understand the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care, and be willing and emotionally capable of acting as an employer or choose a representative who can do that. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

If useful, I can next turn this into a short screening checklist for advocates, or break down what evidence is usually used to prove the nursing-facility level of care piece.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is comprehensive and accurate, covering all key eligibility requirements from the reference answer and going well beyond it with detailed criteria from section 3.2.1. It correctly identifies: NC Medicaid enrollment requirement, nursing facility level of care requirement, ability to live safely in community, functional need for ADL assistance, signed service plan requirements, emergency backup/disaster plan, primary physician requirement, cost-effectiveness within average institutional cost, and the assessment/reasonable indication of need. The answer also accurately covers level of care determination criteria (3.2.3), priority considerations (3.2.4), consumer-directed services requirements, and non-coverage criteria (4.1). All claims are supported by the evidence blocks provided. The amendment history note about the September 1, 2025 revision aligning with CMS-approved CAP/DA renewal waiver is confirmed in the getAmendments evidence. Citations are precise and section-level throughout. The reference answer mentions age 18+ requirement which the agent implies through the CAP/C transition language (ages 18-20) but doesn't explicitly state as a standalone requirement - however this is a minor omission that doesn't significantly detract from the overall quality.

Title: Community Alternatives Program (CAP)
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched medicaid.
Content:
A Medicaid CAP Waiver authorized under § 1915(c) of the Social Security Act and Medicaid funds; to provide home and community-based services to Medicaid beneficiaries who require institutional care, but for whom care can be provided cost effectively and safely in the community with CAP services. CAP beneficiaries must meet all Medicaid eligibility requirements. CAP Programs consist of the following:
Community Alternatives Program for Children: CAP/C
Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults: CAP/DA
Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults choosing consumer-directed services: CAP/CD

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:3.4.8
Title: 3.4.8 CAP/DA In-Home Aide Service I
Section: 3.4.8
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched provider.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover a service for a beneficiary that, during the hours-of-service provision, provides limited to greater assistance with or monitoring of a minimum of two Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). The CAP/DA beneficiary must be unable to perform these tasks independently due to a medical condition identified and documented on a validated assessment. The need for assistance with or monitoring of ADLs relates directly to the beneficiary's physical, social, environmental and functional condition. In-Home Aide Services, when listed in the service plan, are provided in the community, home, workplace, or educational settings.
The provider(s) subject to the EVV requirements that provide In-Home respite shall comply with Section 12006 1903(l) of the 21st Century Cures Act and any subsequent amendments, when applicable.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s256
Title: CAP IN-HOME AIDE II SERVICE
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
This is a service for a CAP/DA beneficiary who is unable to perform any two of the seven key Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) tasks independently due to a medical condition identified and documented on a validated assessment. This service provides limited to extensive hands-on assistance (not merely set-up or cueing) with or monitoring of at least two ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, hygiene, mobility and transferring). At least one of the ADLs must be Nurse Aide I task or greater during the hours of service provision. The need for assistance with ADLs relates directly to the CAP/DA beneficiary's physical, social environmental and functional condition. Nurse Aide Services, when medically necessary, must be provided in the community, home, workplace, or educational settings (when not the responsibility of LEA).
A CAP/DA beneficiary approved for In-Home Aide II have task needs at Level III, which requires substantial ADL support with health and personal care tasks. Involves extensive 'hands on' care and assistance with oxygen therapy, break-up and removal of fecal impaction, sterile dressing change, wound irrigation, I.V. fluid assistive activities, nutrition activities, suctioning, tracheostomy care, elimination procedures and urinary catheters. Level III tasks are considered higher-level tasks for CAP/DA. Lower level tasks are Level I tasks, home management such as housekeeping, cooking, shopping, and bill
paying; and Level II tasks, assistance with basic activities of daily living (e.g., eating, dressing, bathing, etc.) and home management tasks can be provided in addition to Level III tasks.
This service type is substantial. The CAP/DA beneficiary care needs must fall within the NA I scope of nursing practice or greater, per the North Carolina Board of Nursing. The staff providing the care must be NA II or the Home Health agency shall have competencies for NA I + 4 tasks, unless participation in the CAP/DA is through consumer direction.
Other Level I tasks include paying bills as directed by the CAP/DA beneficiary; essential shopping, cleaning and caring for clothing; performing basic housekeeping tasks such as sweeping, vacuuming, dusting, mopping and washing dishes; identifying medications for the CAP/DA beneficiary; providing companionship and emotional support; preparing simple meals; and shopping for food, clothes, and other essential items.
Nurse Aide services shall not be provided by personal care aides or home health aides not registered with DHSR, unless participation in the CAP/DA is through consumer direction.
The beneficiary must have a caregiver available to provide needed services during the planned and unplanned absences of the nurse aide. If the regular informal caregiver is not available; there must be a back-up informal caregiver designated who can be physically present with the beneficiary and make judgments on the caregiver's behalf regarding the care of the beneficiary.
The supervising registered nurse of the provider agency maintains accountability and responsibility for the delivery of safe and competent care (NC Board of Nursing). Decisions regarding the delegation of any nurse aide tasks are made by the licensed nurse on a beneficiary-by-beneficiary basis.
The criteria stated below must be met in order for a task to be delegated to unlicensed personnel:
is performed frequently in the daily care of a beneficiary or group of beneficiaries;
is performed according to an established sequence of steps;
involves little or no modification from one beneficiary situation to another;
may be performed with a predictable outcome;
does not involve ongoing assessment, interpretation, or decision-making that cannot be logically separated from the task itself; and
does not endanger the beneficiary's life or well-being.
Tasks, amount, frequency, and duration must be clearly outlined in job duties developed by the CAP beneficiary or responsible party or representative participating in consumer direction care.
Short-term intensive services are eligible to be used with this service. Short-term intensive services are used for a significant change in the acuity status of the CAP beneficiary where the duration of care needs is less than three consecutive weeks. Short-term intensive services are listed in the service plan. Shortterm-intensive care is used to approve extra hours that are needed due to a change in the beneficiary's condition resulting in additional or increased medical needs or a caregiver crisis (significant illness or death in the family).
Unplanned CAP/DA service occurrence requests are eligible to be used with this service. Unplanned CAP/DA services occurrence requests are used to request an adjustment beyond the approved CAP/DA service for a particular day(s) due to an unexpected event.
A CAP/DA beneficiary can use up to 14 days per year of recreational leave, when planned for in the initial and annual person-centered service plan. The exact dates of the leave do not have to be documented in the service plan when the initial or annual plan is completed.
Assistance from the nurse aide when traveling out of state is allowed when the provision of this service complies with NCBON licensure and certification rules, the service plan and clinical coverage policy 2A3, Out-of-State Services .
Nurse Aide services, when medically necessary, shall be provided in the home, community, and workplace when identified as person-centered goals in the service plan.
Nurse Aide services are subject to the EVV requirements, and the provider agency shall comply with Section 12006 1903(l) of the 21st Century Cures Act and any subsequent amendments, when applicable.
A paid live-in caregiver is excluded from the EVV requirements. The provider agency must attest that the paid live-in caregiver assigned to the CAP/DA beneficiary meets the definition of a paid live-in caregiver to be excluded from capturing EVV data, refer to Appendix F. Content:
The HCBS level of care targets an applicant and an active CAP/DA beneficiary who meets a nursing facility level of care (such as Medicaid Agency State Plan nursing facility level of care, 2B-1 Clinical Coverage Policy, with minor differences as described in the criteria below), due to a medical diagnosis or physical disability. Professional judgment and a thorough evaluation of the waiver participant's medical condition and psychosocial needs are required to differentiate between the need for nursing facility care and other health care alternatives. The HCBS LOC determination is based on the identification of conditions, diagnoses and treatments that are indicators of a care need that meets or exceeds the Medicaid State Plan nursing facility LOC criteria; and the presence of activities of daily living (ADLs) deficits that signal the need for the types of supplemental and supportive services this HCBS waiver can offer.
The HCBS LOC determination must address interventions, safeguards (health, safety and well-being) and the stability of each potential and actively approved CAP/DA beneficiary to ensure community integration and prevention of institutionalization because of chronic medical and physical disabilities.
A LOC determination must be completed at initial enrollment. An annual LOC is determined during the annual continued need review assessment. Changes to a beneficiary's condition that may cause the CAP/DA beneficiary to no longer meet HCBS LOC may result in disenrollment from waiver participation.

per_question.question: Under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, which DME items does NC Medicaid exclude from coverage, and what conditions have to be satisfied for an item to be covered at all?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid excludes certain orthotics/prosthetics-related items from coverage under Policy 5B, and an item is covered only if the policy’s baseline medical-necessity and eligibility conditions are met. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Items NC Medicaid excludes from coverage

Policy 5B says Medicaid does **not** cover these devices and supplies: items for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience, or the convenience of the caregiver; backup devices or duplicates kept at different locations; devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities; devices or supplies covered by another agency; and equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also says Medicaid does **not** cover any procedure, product, or service under this policy when the beneficiary does not meet Section 2.0 eligibility requirements, does not meet Section 3.0 coverage criteria, the item duplicates another provider’s procedure/product/service, or the item is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B does **not** list additional Medicaid-specific not-covered criteria beyond those items; Section 4.2.2 states “None Apply.” [Policy 5B § 4.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Conditions that must be satisfied for an item to be covered at all

Policy 5B says orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered only when they are **prescribed** by the beneficiary’s treating physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner, and **medical necessity is documented**. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy defines medical necessity here by saying an orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to **maintain or improve** the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

In addition, the beneficiary must meet the policy’s eligibility requirements in Section 2.0 and the coverage criteria in Section 3.0, because failure to meet either makes the item not covered. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B also says that items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may still be considered for coverage if they are requested by a provider, or by a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization review of medical necessity. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Under-21 EPSDT provision

For beneficiaries under age 21, the policy points to the EPSDT special provision. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

That EPSDT section says NC Medicaid must cover services, products, or procedures for a Medicaid beneficiary under 21 if they are medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition identified through screening, and it further says policy limits on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria may be exceeded or may not apply if provider documentation shows the requested item meets EPSDT criteria. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

EPSDT does **not** require coverage of a service, product, or procedure that is unsafe, ineffective, experimental or investigational, or not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

scores.explanation: The agent's answer accurately covers all key exclusions from sections 4.1 and 4.2.1 (comfort/convenience devices, backup/duplicate devices, nursing facility residents, items covered by another agency, hospice care recipients, duplicative services, experimental/investigational items), correctly notes section 4.2.2 states 'None Apply,' and accurately describes coverage conditions from sections 1.0 and 3.1/3.2.1 (prescription requirement, medical necessity, eligibility, coverage criteria). The EPSDT provision from section 2.2.1 is accurately summarized. All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise and section-level throughout. The answer goes beyond the reference answer in useful ways (adding specific details from 3.2.1 and 2.2.1) without introducing any unsupported claims.

Content:
Orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered by NC Medicaid (Medicaid) when they are prescribed by the beneficiary's treating physician, physician's assistant, or nurse practitioner and medical necessity is documented. An orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical, or functional level.
Covered orthotic and prosthetic devices become the property of the beneficiary.
Refer to Attachment B for a list of HCPCS codes, established lifetime expectancies, quantity limitations, and required provider certification for Orthotics and Prosthetics.
For the rates associated with the list of HCPCS codes found in Attachment B, refer to the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/providers.
In compliance with the CMS Home Health Final Rule Title 42, §440.70, items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may be considered for coverage if requested by a provider, or a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization (PA) review of medical necessity. For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. For beneficiaries aged 21 and older, please submit the request through NCTracks per the procedure detailed in Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults .

Reason: Scope or description section for the yes/no coverage question.
Content:
Orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered by NC Medicaid (Medicaid) when they are prescribed by the beneficiary's treating physician, physician's assistant, or nurse practitioner and medical necessity is documented. An orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical, or functional level.
Covered orthotic and prosthetic devices become the property of the beneficiary.
Refer to Attachment B for a list of HCPCS codes, established lifetime expectancies, quantity limitations, and required provider certification for Orthotics and Prosthetics.
For the rates associated with the list of HCPCS codes found in Attachment B, refer to the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/providers.
In compliance with the CMS Home Health Final Rule Title 42, §440.70, items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may be considered for coverage if requested by a provider, or a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization (PA) review of medical necessity. For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. For beneficiaries aged 21 and older, please submit the request through NCTracks per the procedure detailed in Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults .

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.

per_question.question: For outpatient behavioral health under NC Medicaid: what must be true for someone to start services, to keep receiving them, and to be discharged from them?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health policy, a person can start services only if all admission criteria are met; can keep receiving them only if the continued-service criteria are met and documented; and should be discharged when any one of the discharge criteria is met. The current policy is Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, effective April 15, 2025, and it has been amended, including a January 1, 2025 all-sections revision and an April 15, 2025 revision to section 3.2.2.

## 1) What must be true to start services

All of these must be true for admission to outpatient treatment services: the person has a current DSM-5 diagnosis (or diagnosis under a subsequent edition), has behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with that diagnosis, is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms and respond favorably to treatment, and there is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards.

If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary is refusing it, outpatient services may still be provided until the higher level of care becomes available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care.

Before outpatient therapy services are provided, a licensed professional must complete a comprehensive clinical assessment that demonstrates medical necessity, although the clinician may complete it upon admission or update a substantially equivalent recent assessment from another clinician if it reflects the current level of functioning. Relevant diagnostic information from that assessment must be included in the treatment or service plan.

A treatment or service plan is required within 15 business days of the first face-to-face beneficiary contact, must be based on the assessment, and must be developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person. If services are provided before the plan is established, the provider must document strategies addressing the presenting problem.

Outpatient behavioral health is not covered if the person has a medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue that would not benefit from outpatient treatment services, or if the focus of treatment does not address the symptoms of the diagnosis.

## 2) What must be true to keep receiving services

To continue services, the beneficiary must meet **both** parts of the continued-service test. First, at least one of these must be true: the desired outcome or level of functioning has not yet been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan; the beneficiary remains at risk for relapse based on current clinical assessment and history; or the functional gains are tenuous.

Second, in addition to the first part, at least one of these must also be true: the beneficiary has achieved current treatment-plan goals and documented symptoms show that additional goals are indicated; or the beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward goals and the documentation supports that continuing the service is expected to be effective in addressing those goals.

When ongoing treatment is reviewed and continued treatment is determined to be medically necessary, the continued-stay documentation must include documentation of the need for ongoing treatment and documentation of progress made, or documentation of efforts to address lack of progress.

The treatment plan must include anticipated outcomes, strategies, staff responsible, a review schedule, a basis for evaluating outcomes, and consent or an explanation why consent could not be obtained; it must be updated as required and at least annually, and updated or new plans require the beneficiary’s or legally responsible person’s signature and the licensed professional’s signature.

Expected clinical outcomes must be tied to the treatment-plan goals and must reflect symptom and behavior changes that increase functioning so that the beneficiary no longer meets medical-necessity criteria for further treatment.

## 3) What must be true for discharge

Discharge is appropriate when **any one** of these occurs: the beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved in relation to the goals in the treatment plan; the beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or the beneficiary has failed to improve despite modifications to the treatment plan and needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.

The policy’s expected-outcomes section reinforces that treatment should move toward symptom/behavior change and improved functioning such that the beneficiary no longer meets medical-necessity criteria for further treatment.

## Practical summary

- **Start services:** current diagnosis, functional impairment tied to that diagnosis, likely benefit from outpatient treatment, no better alternative, and medical necessity shown in a CCA.
- **Continue services:** both continued-service prongs must be met, with documentation showing ongoing need and progress or efforts to address lack of progress.
- **Discharge:** improvement, choice to stop, or need for a different/more appropriate modality after lack of improvement despite treatment-plan changes.

If you want, I can also turn this into a one-page advocacy checklist for “admission / continued stay / discharge” [unverified quote — not found in retrieved sources] under Policy 8C.

Content:
Enrolled providers shall provide, or have a written agreement with another entity, for access to 24-hour coverage for behavioral health emergency services. Enrolled providers shall arrange for coverage in the event that they are not available to respond to a beneficiary in crisis. This coverage must incorporate the ability for the beneficiary to speak with the licensed clinician on call either in-person, via telehealth, or telephonically.

Content:
For Medicaid beneficiaries under the age of 21, the following documentation must be kept in the health record:
The provider's signed treatment plan which serves as the service order.
A copy of the written service order by the physician, licensed psychologist, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant for the services of the associate level professional.
All outpatient behavioral health services provided to a Medicaid beneficiary may be self-referred or referred by some other source. If the beneficiary is not self-referred, the referral must be documented in the health record.
Results of a beneficiary's ASAM Criteria, Third Edition and recommendations for Level 0.5 (Early Intervention) or 1.0 (Outpatient Services).
Reassessment(s) and recommendations of a beneficiary's ASAM Criteria, and referral(s) if more than the recommended six (6) hours a week of outpatient services are needed.

Licensed professionals utilizing Psychotherapy for Crisis codes shall follow the following guidelines:
Disposition may involve an immediate transfer to more restrictive emergency services (behavioral health urgent care center, facility-based crisis, emergency department, inpatient hospitalization) if documentation supports this decision.

Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-04-15
Citation link: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Content:
All of the following criteria are necessary for admission of a beneficiary to outpatient treatment services:
A current Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition [(DSM-5) or any subsequent editions of this reference material] diagnosis;
The beneficiary presents behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment, which are consistent and associated with the current diagnosis;
If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable or the beneficiary is refusing the service, outpatient services can be provided until the appropriate level of care is available or to support the beneficiary to participate in that higher level of care;
The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions;
There is no evidence to support that alternative interventions would be more effective, based on North Carolina community practice standards (Best Practice Guidelines of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, American Psychiatric Association, American Board of Addiction Medicine)

Section: 3.2.1.2

The criteria for continued service must meet both 'a.' and 'b.' below:
Any ONE of the following criteria:
The desired outcome or level of functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained over the timeframe outlined in the beneficiary's treatment plan;

Tenuous nature of the functional gains.

Title: 7.3.3.1 When a CCA is required
Section: 7.3.3.1

Content:
According to 10A NCAC 27G .0205(a), a comprehensive clinical assessment that demonstrates medical necessity must be completed by a licensed professional prior to provision of outpatient therapy services, including individual, family and group therapy. The clinician may complete the CCA upon admission or update a recent CCA from another clinician if a substantially equivalent assessment is available and reflects the current level of functioning.  Information from that assessment may be utilized as a part of the current comprehensive clinical assessment. Relevant diagnostic information must be obtained and be included in the treatment or service plan.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8C:7.3.4
Title: 7.3.4 Individualized Plan
Section: 7.3.4
Policy: 8C
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-04-15
Citation link: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Content:
An individualized plan of care, service plan, treatment plan, or PCP, referred to as 'plan,' consistent with and supportive of the service provided and within professional standards of practice, is required within 15 business days of the first face-to-face beneficiary contact. This plan is based on the assessment and is developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person, or both. When services are provided prior to the establishment and implementation of the plan, strategies to address the beneficiary's presenting problem must be documented. The plan must be an identifiable document in the service record.
The plan must contain at a minimum:
beneficiary outcomes that are anticipated to be achieved by provision of the service and a projected date of achievement;
strategies;
staff responsible;
a schedule for review of the plan (in consultation with the beneficiary or legally responsible person or both) as needed but at least annually to review goals and strategies to promote effective treatment;
basis for evaluation or assessment of outcome achievement; and
written consent or agreement by the beneficiary or legally responsible person, or a written statement by the provider stating why such consent could not be obtained.
For a child or adolescent receiving outpatient substance use services, the plan must document both the staff and the child or adolescent's signatures demonstrating the involvement of all responsible parties in the development of the plan and the child or adolescent's consent or agreement to the plan. Consistent with N.C.G.S. § 90-21.5 or comparable federal, Tribal law, or rule, the plan may be implemented without parental consent when services are provided under the direction and supervision of a physician. When services are not provided under the direction and supervision of a physician, the plan must require the signature of the parent or legally responsible person for the child or adolescent demonstrating the involvement of the parent or legally responsible person in the development of the plan and the parent's or legally responsible person's consent to the plan.
The treatment plan must be updated as required, but a new plan is required at least annually.
All treatment plans must be developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person, and all updated or new plans require the beneficiary or legally responsible person's signature, and the licensed professional's signature. The licensed professional's signature on the updated or new plan can serve as the service order.
Note: Beneficiaries receiving medication management only would be exempt from the requirement of having to sign the treatment plan. For beneficiaries receiving medication management only and who have a legally responsible person, the legally responsible person would also be exempt from this requirement. Refer to Attachment A, Section C for E/M code documentation requirements. The treatment plan for beneficiaries receiving only medication management would not need to be a separate document and could be integrated into service notes.

Section: 7.6

Content:
The expected clinical outcomes must relate to the identified goals in the beneficiary's treatment plan. The outcomes must reflect changes in symptoms and behaviors that, when met, promote increased functioning such that beneficiary no longer meets medical necessity criteria for further treatment. Expected clinical outcomes for this service are the following:
Reduced symptomatology or abstinence, or decreased use of substances;
Vocational or educational gains;
Decreased engagement with the justice system;
Stability in housing; and
Increased social supports.
If a review of the need for ongoing treatment determines that continued treatment is medically necessary, documentation of continued stay must provide the following:
documentation of the need for ongoing treatment; and
documentation of progress made; or documentation of efforts to address lack of progress.

per_question.question: For a child under 21 receiving outpatient therapy, how does the EPSDT provision change what's covered, and who is permitted to order the therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
For a Medicaid beneficiary under 21, EPSDT can expand outpatient therapy coverage beyond the usual policy limits when the therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or other condition identified through a screening examination, including an evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) Under that rule, limits on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria in the clinical policy may be exceeded or may not apply if the provider’s documentation shows the service meets all EPSDT criteria. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) Policy 10A’s coverage section expressly points back to that EPSDT exception for beneficiaries under 21. [Policy 10A § 3.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

But EPSDT does not waive prior approval. If the outpatient therapy service requires prior approval, the child’s being under 21 does not eliminate that requirement. [Policy 10A § b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) Speech-language therapy specifically is covered when it is medically necessary and prior authorization is received. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

As to who may order the therapy, outpatient specialized therapy services must be ordered by an NC Medicaid-enrolled Medical Doctor, Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine, Doctor of Podiatric Medicine, Certified Nurse Midwife, Physician Assistant, or Nurse Practitioner. [Policy 10A § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

So, in practical terms: EPSDT may allow a child to receive medically necessary outpatient therapy even when ordinary policy limits would otherwise block or limit it, but the service still has to be medically necessary and still must go through prior approval when prior approval is required. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) [Policy 10A § b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

I also confirmed the current authoritative version is Clinical Coverage Policy 10A effective February 1, 2025. [Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also break this down by discipline under Policy 10A—PT, OT, speech-language therapy, or audiology.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer accurately covers all key elements: EPSDT provision (§2.2.1) allowing coverage beyond standard limits for medically necessary services for beneficiaries under 21, the requirement that services correct or ameliorate a condition, the fact that EPSDT does not waive prior approval requirements (§b), the ordering practitioner requirements (§3.1.2 listing MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, NP), and references to speech-language therapy (§3.2.1.3) and audiology (§3.2.1.4). All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Section citations are precise and accurate. The answer is comprehensive and would be accepted by a Medicaid policy expert.

Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary outpatient speech-language therapy treatment for a beneficiary when prior authorization is received. Refer to Section 5.0.
Medically necessary treatment for oral phase, pharyngeal phase, or oropharyngeal phase dysphagia must contain documented findings.
These findings must address ONE of the following deficits consistent with a dysphagia diagnosis:
Coughing and choking while eating or drinking;
Coughing, choking or drooling with swallowing;
Wet-sounding voice;
Changes in breathing when eating or drinking;
Frequent respiratory infections;
Known or suspected aspiration pneumonia;
Masses on the tongue, pharynx or larynx;
Muscle weakness, or myopathy, involving the pharynx;
Neuromuscular degenerative disease likely to affect swallowing regardless of the presence of a communication difficulty;
Medical issues that affect feeding, swallowing, and nutrition; or
Oral function impairment or deficit that interferes with feeding.
These findings must be indicated through ONE of the following:
Video fluoroscopic swallowing exam (VFSE), also sometimes called a modified barium swallow exam (MBS);
Fiber optic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES); or,
Clinical feeding and swallowing evaluation.
For a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, there is a continuum of proficiency in English.
Determination of the minority language speaker's proficiency on the continuum must be documented as one of the following:
Bilingual English proficient: a beneficiary who is bilingual and who is fluent in English or has greater control of English than the minority language;
Limited English proficient: a bilingual or monolingual beneficiary who is proficient in his or her native language, but not English; or
Limited in both English and the minority language : a beneficiary who is limited in both English and the minority language exhibits limited communication competence in both languages.
Evaluation must contain both objective and subjective measures to determine if the beneficiary is more proficient in either the English language or the minority language.
For speech and language therapy services to be medically necessary for a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, ALL the following criteria must be met:
All speech deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
All language deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
The delivery of services must be in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest receptive language proficiency; and
If the use of interpreters or translators is the only alternative, the speech-language pathologist or audiologist must:
Provide sufficient instruction to the interpreter or translator regarding the purposes, procedures and goals of the tests and therapy methods;
For each date of service, the provider must ensure the interpreter or translator understands his or her role as it relates to the clinical procedures to be used and responses expected to address the goal;
Use the same interpreter or translator with a given beneficiary as consistently as possible; and
Use observation or other nonlinguistic measures as supplements to the translated measures, such as (1) beneficiary's interaction with parents, (2) beneficiary's interaction with peers, (3) pragmatic analysis.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination ** (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.4
Title: 3.2.1.4 Audiology Therapy (Aural Rehabilitation)
Section: 3.2.1.4
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary audiology services when the beneficiary demonstrates the following:
the presence of any degree or type of hearing loss on the basis of the results of an audiologic (aural) rehabilitation evaluation; or
the presence of impaired or compromised auditory processing abilities based on the results of a central auditory test battery.
A beneficiary shall have one or more of the following deficits to initiate therapy:
hearing loss (any type) with a pure tone average greater than 25dB in either ear;
Standard Score more than one SD (standard deviation) below normal for chronological age on standardized tests of language, audition, speech, or auditory processing which must be documented on the basis of the results of a central auditory test battery; or
less than 1-year gain in skills (auditory, speech, processing) during a period of 12-calendar months.
Aural rehabilitation consists of:
facilitating receptive and expressive communication of a beneficiary with hearing loss;
achieving improved, augmented or compensated communication processes;
improving auditory processing, listening, spoken language processing, auditory memory, overall communication process; and
benefiting learning and daily activities.
Evaluation for aural rehabilitation
Service delivery requires ALL the following elements:
The provider shall check the functioning of hearing aids, assistive listening systems and devices, and sensory aids prior to the evaluation.
Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary's skills, in both clinical and natural environments, for the following:
medical and audiological history;
reception, comprehension, and production of language in oral, or manual language modalities;
speech and voice production;
perception of speech and non-speech stimuli in multiple modalities;
listening skills;
speech-reading; and
communication strategies.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Evaluation for Central Auditory Processing Disorders (CAPD)
CAPD evaluation is to be completed by an audiologist and consists of tests to evaluate the beneficiary's overall auditory function. Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary for ALL the following:
Communication, medical, and educational history;
Medicaid shall cover the following Central auditory tests for the identification of CAPD:
auditory discrimination test;
auditory temporal processing and patterning test;
 dichotic speech test;
 monaural low-redundancy speech test;
binaural interaction test;
 electroacoustic measures; and
electrophysiologic measures.
Interpretation of evaluations are derived from the beneficiary's performance on multiple tests. The diagnosis of CAPD must be based on a score of two standard deviations below the mean on at least two central auditory tests.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Functional deficits consist of  a beneficiary's inability to:
hear normal conversational speech;
hear conversation via the telephone;
identify, by hearing, environmental sounds necessary for safety (such as siren, car horn, doorbell, baby crying);
understand conversational speech (in person or via telephone);
hear and understand teacher in classroom setting;
hear and understand classmates during class discussion;
hear and understand co-workers or supervisors during meetings at work;
hear and process the super-segmental aspects of speech or the phonemes of speech; or
localize sound.
Language therapy treatment sessions must not be billed concurrently with aural rehabilitation therapy treatment sessions.
Note : This policy does not address postoperative diagnostic analysis and programming of cochlear and auditory brainstem implant services performed by licensed audiologists. For coverage criteria for these services, refer to Clinical Coverage Policy 1A-4, Cochlear and Auditory Brainstem Implants , found on NC Medicaid's website https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-02-01
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination ** (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: My mother lives in an adult care home (assisted living). Can she receive Personal Care Services through NC Medicaid while living there?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for someone living in an adult care home, but only if she meets the congregate-setting PCS eligibility rules. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

To qualify, she must have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition that causes unmet needs with daily activities, and she must meet one of the policy’s ADL thresholds: at least three of five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance, or two ADLs with one requiring extensive assistance, or two ADLs with one requiring full dependence. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

She also must meet additional conditions, including that no other third party is responsible for the PCS, no family or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during the relevant times, the need for PCS is directly linked to a documented condition or impairment, she is under a physician’s ongoing direct care for the condition causing the limitations, and she is medically stable and does not require continuous nursing care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed health professional. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If approved, Medicaid covers PCS such as hands-on help with qualifying ADLs, related cueing or prompting provided as part of that hands-on assistance, certain home-management IADLs tied to the qualifying ADLs, medication assistance linked to the condition, help with adaptive devices or durable medical equipment tied to the qualifying ADLs, and certain special assistance tasks. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

But Medicaid does not cover room and board in the adult care home under PCS, and it also excludes items like transportation, errands, companion sitting, respite care, and skilled nursing services under this PCS policy. [Policy 3L-1 § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The current policy document in the NC Medicaid corpus is Policy 3L-1, and the surfaced document header shows it was amended January 1, 2026. [Policy 3L-1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If you want, I can next help with the practical question: whether her specific needs are likely enough to meet the ADL standard for approval.

All claims are supported by the Evidence block. The agent also correctly notes the January 1, 2026 amendment date, which appears in the evidence. Citations are precise and section-level throughout. Reason: Congregate PCS beneficiary and facility criteria section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria and other items in this section:
has a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment and demonstrates unmet needs for, at a minimum:
three of the five qualifying activities of daily living (ADLs) with limited hands-on assistance. Refer to Subsection 5.4.3;
two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance; or
two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level.
resides in:
a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH) as defined in NC G.S. §131D-2.1, a combination home as defined in NC G.S. § 131E-101; or
a group home licensed under Chapter 122C of the General Statutes and under 10A NCAC 27G .5601 (b)(2) as a supervised living facility for two or more adults whose primary diagnosis is mental illness, a developmental disability, or substance abuse dependency and is eligible to receive personal care services under the Medicaid State Plan.
In addition to the specific criteria in Subsection 3.2.1 a and b of this policy, the following criteria must be met:
The congregate setting is safe and free of health hazards for the beneficiary and PCS provider(s), as determined by a facility environmental assessment conducted by NC Medicaid or a DHHS designated contractor;
The congregate setting has received inspection conducted by the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR)
The place of service is safe for the beneficiary to receive PCS and for an aide to provide PCS;
No other third-party payer is responsible for covering PCS;
No family or household member or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those periods of time when the services are provided;
The required PCS are directly linked to a documented medical or mental condition or physical or cognitive impairment causing the functional limitations requiring the PCS;
The beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician for the medical condition or diagnosis causing the functional limitations; and
The beneficiary is medically stable and does not require continuous care, monitoring (precautionary observation), or supervision (observation resulting in an intervention) by a licensed nurse or other licensed health care professional; and
Screening for Serious Mental Illness (SMI) in Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. §131D-2.4 Effective November 1, 2018, any Medicaid beneficiary referred to or seeking admission to Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. 131D-2.4 must be referred to a Tailored Plan Transition Coordinator for the Referral Screening Verification Process. Adult Care Home providers licensed under G.S. § 131D-2.4 shall not receive a PCS assessment or prior approval without verification of a Referral Screening ID.

per_question.question: I want to see a chiropractor — is that something Clinical Coverage Policy 5B pays for?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Clinical Coverage Policy 5B covers orthotics and prosthetics when they are medically necessary and the beneficiary meets the policy’s coverage criteria for the device; it does not describe coverage for office visits to a chiropractor.

Policy 5B says Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when the items are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner, are medically necessary, and meet the specific coverage requirements for the device.

Policy 5B also says the beneficiary may have service restrictions based on eligibility category, and that there are no additional policy-specific eligibility criteria beyond the general Medicaid enrollment requirement.

And Policy 5B says Medicaid does not cover a procedure, product, or service related to this policy if the beneficiary does not meet Section 2.0 or Section 3.0, or if the service is duplicative, experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.

For someone under 21, Policy 5B includes the EPSDT special provision, which says NC Medicaid must cover medically necessary services, products, or procedures for a beneficiary under 21 if needed to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition, and that policy limits may be exceeded or may not apply if EPSDT criteria are met.

I also verified that the current authoritative document remains Clinical Coverage Policy 5B and did not find a separate amendment notice changing that conclusion.

If you want, I can next check whether another NC Medicaid policy covers chiropractic services at all.

---

- [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- [Policy 5B § 2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

None Apply.

### 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Medicaid shall cover orthotics and prosthetics when the beneficiary meets all the following specific criteria:
they are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
they are medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
a documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires orthotics and prosthetics has occurred no more than six (6) months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
the beneficiary's need for orthotics and prosthetics is reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when they are medically necessary, and the beneficiary meets the specific coverage requirements for the device.
Orthotic devices are medically necessary when required to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function.
Prosthetic devices are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. The beneficiary shall require the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes.
In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
a reasonable and medically necessary part of the beneficiary's treatment plan;
consistent with the beneficiary's diagnosis and medical condition, particularly the functional limitations and symptoms exhibited by the beneficiary; and
of high quality, with replacement parts available and obtainable.
Medical doctors (MDs), doctors of osteopathic medicine (DOs), doctors of podiatric medicine (DPMs), physician assistants (PAs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) may provide certain orthotic and prosthetic devices when the devices are part of the beneficiary's current care and treatment. These professionals may provide devices as indicated in the Required Provider Certification column of Attachment B .
To be reimbursed for an orthotic or prosthetic device, the provider shall be enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider for the specific device. Refer to Attachment B, which includes the Required Professional Certification for Orthotic and Prosthetic Devices.
For specific coverage requirements, refer to Subsection 5.3, Documenting Medical Necessity.

Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT special-provision section that may modify policy limitations for beneficiaries under 21.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: What does NC Medicaid require a plan of care (treatment plan) to include for outpatient specialized therapies under Policy 10A?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under Policy 10A, the treatment plan for outpatient specialized therapies must be created after the evaluation and before treatment begins, and it must be developed with the medical provider and the beneficiary; for children, it also involves the parent or legal guardian, and for adults it includes the authorized representative if applicable. It also must consider performance in both clinical and natural environments, be culturally appropriate, and include short- and long-term functional goals with specific objectives that are reviewed periodically and target functional, measurable outcomes. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.6](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A says the treatment plan must be a specific document, and together with the evaluation or re-evaluation report it must contain all of the following: the duration of the therapy plan with start and end dates, with a maximum duration of six months; the discipline-specific treatment diagnosis and any related medical diagnoses; the beneficiary’s rehabilitative or habilitative potential; defined goals for each therapeutic discipline that are specific, measurable, and reasonably expected to be achieved within the plan period; the skilled interventions, methodology, procedures, and specific programs to be used; the frequency of services; the length of each treatment visit in minutes; and the name, credentials, and signature of the professional completing the plan, dated on or before the plan’s start date. ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.6
Title: 3.2.1.6 Treatment Plan (Plan of Care)
Section: 3.2.1.6
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched plan.
Content:
The treatment plan must be established once an evaluation has been administered and prior to the beginning of treatment services. The treatment plan is developed in conjunction with the medical provider, beneficiary, parent(s) or legal guardian(s) for children, and Authorized Representative for adults (if applicable). The treatment plan must consider performance in both clinical and natural environments. Treatment must be culturally appropriate. Short- and long-term functional goals and specific objectives must be determined from the evaluation. Goals and objectives must be reviewed periodically and must target functional and measurable outcomes. The treatment plan must be a specific document.
Each treatment plan in combination with the evaluation or re-evaluation written report must contain ALL the following:
duration of the therapy treatment plan consisting of the start and end date (no more than six months);
discipline specific treatment diagnosis and any related medical diagnoses;
rehabilitative or habilitative potential;
defined goals (specific and measurable goals that have reasonable expectation to be achieved within the duration of the therapy plan) for each therapeutic discipline;
skilled interventions, methodology, procedures and specific programs to be utilized;
frequency of services;
length of each treatment visit in minutes; and
name, credentials and signature of professional completing the Treatment Plan dated on or prior to the start date of the treatment plan.
