per_question.question: Federal law sets a minimum medical loss ratio for Medicaid managed care plans — what is that requirement, and how has North Carolina implemented it?
per_question.agent_answer:
Federal law does **not** impose a universal Medicaid managed-care minimum MLR on every state. Instead, federal law requires states to make Medicaid managed care plans **calculate and report** an MLR under the federal methodology, and it says that **if a state chooses to require a minimum MLR, that minimum must be at least 85%**. [42 CFR § 438.8(c) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.74 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Federal rule

States must ensure, through their Medicaid managed-care contracts, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR in accordance with 42 C.F.R. § 438.8. That requirement applies to contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017, with a transition rule for certain multi-year contracts. [42 CFR § 438.8(a) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The federal minimum-threshold rule is conditional: **if** a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs, the minimum MLR must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. [42 CFR § 438.8(c) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

Federal oversight then requires the state to submit to CMS an annual summary for each contracted MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that includes at least the **numerator amount, denominator amount, MLR percentage achieved, member months, and any remittances owed** for the reporting year. [42 CFR § 438.74(a)(1)-(2) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

If a state contract requires remittances because a plan failed to meet the state’s minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the **federal share** of that remittance and must separately report the methodology used to determine the state and federal shares. [42 CFR § 438.74(b)(1)-(2) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The core federal methodology defines MLR as the ratio of a **numerator** to a **denominator**, with a possible **credibility adjustment**. The numerator includes incurred claims, expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, and fraud prevention activities, while the denominator is addressed in § 438.8(f) as adjusted premium revenue after specified deductions such as taxes and licensing or regulatory fees. [42 CFR § 438.8(d)-(e)(1) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.8(e)(2)(ii)-(v) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The federal text also shows recent revision history: § 438.74 was amended at **89 Fed. Reg. 41276 (May 10, 2024)**, and § 438.8 was amended at **89 Fed. Reg. 41272 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR § 438.74 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

In the BH I/DD Tailored Plan contract amendment surfaced here, North Carolina implemented the federal framework by requiring the plan to **calculate and report aggregate MLR annually**, aligned to the rating year, on **two bases**: a **CMS-defined MLR** and a **Department-defined MLR**. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

For the **CMS-defined MLR**, North Carolina expressly incorporates the federal methodology in **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**, requires reporting in the aggregate for **Medicaid Expansion eligible members and non-expansion populations combined**, and defines the numerator as incurred claims plus health-care-quality expenditures plus the lesser of fraud-reduction expenditures or fraud-reduction recoveries. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

The same North Carolina contract section defines the **CMS-defined MLR denominator** as adjusted premium revenue, meaning premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing and regulatory fees, again tracking the federal rule. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

North Carolina also adds a separate **Department-defined MLR** for **non-expansion populations**. That measure is calculated similarly to the CMS-defined MLR but allows certain voluntary contributions to health-related resources and public-health or Health Equity initiatives if they meet Department Quality Strategy standards, and it excludes certain directed or wrap payments and related-provider payments that violate contract payment limitations. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

For both the CMS-defined and Department-defined MLRs, North Carolina requires Department review and approval of classifications for activities that improve health care quality and public-health or Health Equity initiatives. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

North Carolina also requires both MLR calculations to exclude from the numerator items such as **interest or penalty payments to providers for prompt-pay failures, fines and penalties, certain rebates or remittance-substitute contributions, non-claims costs, PBM fees and spread pricing, marketing or branding materials, related-party administrative payments and margin, and administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement**. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

The contract further requires aggregation of data across all Medicaid eligibility groups for the CMS-defined MLR and all non-expansion eligibility groups for the Department-defined MLR, and it applies a **credibility adjustment** for plans with **less than 380,000 member months** in an MLR reporting year. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

The surfaced North Carolina contract text also states that **Healthy Opportunities Pilot Program payments are not incorporated into capitation or into the MLR unless CMS requires otherwise**. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

So the short answer is: federal law requires Medicaid managed-care plans to **calculate and report** MLR under a federal formula, and if a state chooses to set a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR § 438.8(a), (c) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

In the North Carolina implementation surfaced here, the state contract adopts the **federal CMS-defined MLR methodology** and layers on a separate **Department-defined MLR** for certain populations, with additional state-specific inclusion, exclusion, aggregation, and review rules. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

I could verify North Carolina’s implementation in the **BH I/DD Tailored Plan** contract section that was surfaced here, but I did **not** retrieve a separate North Carolina contract section in this answer showing whether the state has imposed the same minimum-threshold terms across all other Medicaid managed-care plan types. [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is highly accurate and well-supported by the evidence. It correctly identifies that federal law (42 CFR § 438.8) requires MCOs to calculate and report MLR, and that if a state mandates a minimum MLR, it must be at least 85%. This nuance (that the 85% floor is conditional on the state electing to mandate a minimum) is actually more precise than the reference answer. The agent accurately describes NC's implementation through the BH I/DD Tailored Plan contract, including the dual MLR framework (CMS-defined and Department-defined), numerator/denominator definitions, exclusions, credibility adjustments (380,000 member months threshold), aggregation rules, and Healthy Opportunities Pilot Program treatment — all directly supported by the evidence block. Citations are precise, referencing specific CFR sections (438.8, 438.74) and the specific NC contract amendment. The agent appropriately flags the limitation that it only verified the BH I/DD Tailored Plan contract and not all NC managed care plan types. No hallucinations detected against the evidence provided.

Content:
(a) State reporting requirement. (1) The State must annually submit to CMS a summary description of each report(s) received from the MCO(s), PIHP(s), and PAHP(s) under contract with the State, according to § 438.8(k), with the rate certification required in § 438.7.

(2) The summary description must be provided for each MCO, PIHP, or PAHP under contract with the State and must include, at a minimum, the amount of the numerator, the amount of the denominator, the MLR percentage achieved, the number of member months, and any remittances owed by each MCO, PIHP, or PAHP for that MLR reporting year.

(b) Repayment of Federal share of remittances. (1) If a State requires a MCO, PIHP, or PAHP to pay remittances through the contract for not meeting the minimum MLR required by the State, the State must reimburse CMS for an amount equal to the Federal share of the remittance, taking into account applicable differences in the Federal matching rate.

(2) If a remittance is owed according to paragraph (b)(1) of this section, the State must submit a separate report describing the methodology used to determine the State and Federal share of the remittance with the report required in paragraph (a) of this section.

ID: sec:doc:federal_regulation:42-CFR-438:438.8
Title: Medical loss ratio (MLR) standards
Section: 438.8
Policy: 42-CFR-438
Type: federal_regulation
Last revised: 2024-05-10
Federal Register cite: [81 FR 27853, May 6, 2016, as amended at 82 FR 39, Jan. 3, 2017; 85 FR 72840, Nov. 13, 2020; 89 FR 41272, May 10, 2024]
Citation link: [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
Reason: Primary MLR calculation or reporting section from the governing regulation.
Content:
(a) Basic rule. The State must ensure, through its contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP calculate and report a MLR in accordance with this section. For multi-year contracts that do not start in 2017, the State must require the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP to calculate and report a MLR for the rating period that begins in 2017.

(b) Definitions. As used in this section, the following terms have the indicated meanings:

Credibility adjustment means an adjustment to the MLR for a partially credible MCO, PIHP, or PAHP to account for a difference between the actual and target MLRs that may be due to random statistical variation.

Full credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be sufficient for the calculation of a MLR with a minimal chance that the difference between the actual and target medical loss ratio is not statistically significant. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned full credibility (or is fully credible) will not receive a credibility adjustment to its MLR.

Member months mean the number of months an enrollee or a group of enrollees is covered by an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP over a specified time period, such as a year.

MLR reporting year means a period of 12 months consistent with the rating period selected by the State.

No credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be insufficient for the calculation of a MLR. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned no credibility (or is non-credible) will not be measured against any MLR requirements.

Non-claims costs means those expenses for administrative services that are not: Incurred claims (as defined in paragraph (e)(2) of this section); expenditures on activities that improve health care quality (as defined in paragraph (e)(3) of this section); or licensing and regulatory fees, or Federal and State taxes (as defined in paragraph (f)(2) of this section).

Partial credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be sufficient for the calculation of a MLR but with a non-negligible chance that the difference between the actual and target medical loss ratios is statistically significant. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned partial credibility (or is partially credible) will receive a credibility adjustment to its MLR.

(c) MLR requirement. If a State elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs, that minimum MLR must be equal to or higher than 85 percent (the standard used for projecting actuarial soundness under § 438.4(b)) and the MLR must be calculated and reported for each MLR reporting year by the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP, consistent with this section.

(d) Calculation of the MLR. The MLR experienced for each MCO, PIHP, or PAHP in a MLR reporting year is the ratio of the numerator (as defined in paragraph (e) of this section) to the denominator (as defined in paragraph (f) of this section). A MLR may be increased by a credibility adjustment, in accordance with paragraph (h) of this section.

(e) Numerator —(1) Required elements. The numerator of an MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's MLR for a MLR reporting year is the sum of the MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's incurred claims (as defined in (e)(2) of this section); the MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's expenditures for activities that improve health care quality (as defined in paragraph (e)(3) of this section); and fraud prevention activities (as defined in paragraph (e)(4) of this section).

(2) Incurred claims. (i) Incurred claims must include the following:

(A) Direct claims that the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP paid to providers (including under capitated contracts with network providers) for services or supplies covered under the contract and services meeting the requirements of § 438.3(e) provided to enrollees.

(B) Unpaid claims liabilities for the MLR reporting year, including claims reported that are in the process of being adjusted or claims incurred but not reported.

(C) Withholds from payments made to network providers.

(D) Claims that are recoverable for anticipated coordination of benefits.

(E) Claims payments recoveries received as a result of subrogation.

(F) Incurred but not reported claims based on past experience, and modified to reflect current conditions, such as changes in exposure or claim frequency or severity.

(G) Changes in other claims-related reserves.

(H) Reserves for contingent benefits and the medical claim portion of lawsuits.

(ii) Amounts that must be deducted from incurred claims include the following:

(A) Overpayment recoveries received from network providers.

(B) Prescription drug rebates received and accrued.

(iii) Expenditures that must be included in incurred claims include the following:

(A) The amount of incentive and bonus payments made, or expected to be made, to network providers that are tied to clearly-defined, objectively measurable, and well-documented clinical or quality improvement standards that apply to providers.

(B) The amount of claims payments recovered through fraud reduction efforts, not to exceed the amount of fraud reduction expenses. The amount of fraud reduction expenses must not include activities specified in paragraph (e)(4) of this section.

(C) The amount of payments made to providers under State directed payments described in § 438.6(c).

(iv) Amounts that must either be included in or deducted from incurred claims include, respectively, net payments or receipts related to State mandated solvency funds.

(v) Amounts that must be excluded from incurred claims:

(A) Non-claims costs, as defined in paragraph (b) of this section, which include the following:

( 1 ) Amounts paid to third party vendors for secondary network savings.

( 2 ) Amounts paid to third party vendors for network development, administrative fees, claims processing, and utilization management.

(i) The Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) standards are to ensure the BH I/DD Tailored Plan is directing a sufficient portion of the capitation payments received from the Department to services and activities that improve health in alignment with the Department's program goals and objectives.
(ii) The BH I/DD Tailored Plan shall calculate and report aggregate MLR on an annual basis aligned to the rating year on two (2) bases as follows:
(a) The BH I/DD Tailored Plan shall calculate the CMS-defined MLR experienced in a MLR reporting year as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8 and 42 C.F.R § 457.1203(c)-(f).
The CMS-defined MLR shall be reported in aggregate combined for Medicaid Expansion Eligible Member and non-Medicaid Expansion populations.
The numerator of the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's CMS -defined MLR for a MLR reporting year shall be defined as the sum of the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's incurred claims, expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, and the lesser of expenditures for fraud reduction activities or fraud reduction recoveries as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e).
The denominator of the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's CMS -defined MLR for a MLR reporting year shall equal the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's adjusted premium revenue. The adjusted premium revenue shall be defined as the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's premium revenue minus the BH I/DD Tailored Plan's federal, state, and local taxes and licensing and regulatory fees as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(f).
(b) The  BH  I/DD  Tailored  Plan  shall  calculate  the  Department-defined  MLR  experienced  for  all  Non-Expansion populations in a MLR reporting year as the ratio of the numerator and denominator.
Reserved.
The numerator of the Department-defined MLR shall be calculated in a manner similar to the CMS-defined MLR with the following adjustments:
The BH I/DD Tailored Plan is permitted to include expenditures made for voluntary contributions to health-related resources and initiatives that advance public health and Health Equity that align with the Department's Quality Strategy and meet the followin g conditions:

Title: i. Disenrollment from BH I/DD Tailored Plans and Medicaid Managed Care
Type: managed_care_contract
Citation link: [Contract #30-2020-052-DHB-TP Amendment 5/7](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-2020-052-dhb-tp-amendment-57/download?attachment)
Reason: State implementation section from the NC policy document named by the question.
Content:
Member disenrollment from the BH I/DD Tailored Plan may occur pursuant to specific criteria described in this Policy, which may include complete disenrollment from Medicaid Managed Care or disenrolling from a BH I/DD Tailored Plan to a Standard Plan.
Member requested disenrollment
A member, or an authorized representative, may submit a verbal or written request for disenrollment from the BH I/DD Tailored Plan to the Enrollment Broker by phone, mail, inperson, or electronically.
A member who is not excluded from Standard Plan enrollment may request disenrollment from a BH I/DD Tailored Plan and transfer to a Standard Plan or the EBCI Tribal Option (if applicable) any time during the coverage year. 11 2
A member who is excluded from Standard Plan enrollment may request disenrollment from a BH I/DD Tailored Plan and transfer  to  NC Medicaid Direct  any  time during  the coverage year.
10 2 There may be instances (e.g., an urgent medical need), as determined by the Department and based on the beneficiary's needs, in which enrollment in the new PHP or the new delivery system may become effective sooner, including mid-month.
11 1 Members enrolled in the Innovations or TBI waivers must disenroll from their respective waiver before they can disenroll from a BH I/DD Tailored Plan.
The member, or the authorized representative, must contact the Enrollment Broker in order to initiate a disenrollment request.
At the time of the disenrollment request, choice counseling for the member or his or her representative will be available from the Enrollment Broker.
The  Enrollment  Broker  will  process  disenrollment  requests  in  accordance  with  the following:
The Enrollment Broker will evaluate the request and will approve it if the member is not enrolled in the Innovations or TBI waiver.
The Enrollment Broker will notify the Department of its decision by the next business day following receipt of the request.
Notice of disenrollment determination
The Department will notify the member or authorized representative, and the BH I/DD Tailored Plan of the approval or denial of the disenrollment request and, if approved, the disenrollment will be effective the first day of the month following receipt of the request by the Enrollment Broker.
The effective date of an approved disenrollment request will be no later than the first day of the second month following the month in which the member requests disenrollment. If the  Enrollment  Broker  or the Department fails to make a disenrollment determination within the specified timeframes, the disenrollment is considered approved for the first day of the following month unless there is an urgent need. 12 1
Expedited review of member initiated requests for disenrollment
A member, or an authorized representative, may request an expedited review of his or her disenrollment request when the member has an urgent medical need. For purposes of this subsection, an urgent medical need means continued enrollment in the BH I/DD Tailored Plan could jeopardize the member's life, physical or mental health, or ability to attain, maintain, or regain maximum function.
The Enrollment Broker will process requests for expedited review in accordance with the following:
The Enrollment Broker will transmit expedited review requests to the Department for evaluation within twelve (12) hours of receipt of the request.
The  Department  will  evaluate  and  decide  whether  to  approve  or  deny  the request.
The Department will notify the member, or authorized representative, and the BH I/DD Tailored Plan of the approval or denial of the expedited disenrollment request. If approved, the disenrollment effective date, will be within three (3) calendar days of receipt of the request by the Enrollment Broker.

The Department may disenroll a member from Medicaid Managed Care for any of the following reasons:
(a) Loss of eligibility
If the Department determines that a member is no longer eligible for Medicaid, the  member  will  be  notified  by  the  Department  and  the  member  will  be

disenrolled from the BH I/DD Tailored Plan. The disenrollment effective date will be the last date of the member's Medicaid eligibility.
If  a  member  is  disenrolled  from  a  BH  I/DD  Tailored  Plan  solely  because  the member loses his or her eligibility for Medicaid for a period of two (2) months or less, the member will automatically be reenrolled in the BH I/DD Tailored Plan upon reenrollment in Medicaid. 13 1

ID: sec:doc:federal_regulation:42-CFR-438:438.8
Title: Medical loss ratio (MLR) standards
Section: 438.8
Policy: 42-CFR-438
Type: federal_regulation
Last revised: 2024-05-10
Federal Register cite: [81 FR 27853, May 6, 2016, as amended at 82 FR 39, Jan. 3, 2017; 85 FR 72840, Nov. 13, 2020; 89 FR 41272, May 10, 2024]
Citation link: [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

Content:
(a) Basic rule. The State must ensure, through its contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP calculate and report a MLR in accordance with this section. For multi-year contracts that do not start in 2017, the State must require the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP to calculate and report a MLR for the rating period that begins in 2017.

(b) Definitions. As used in this section, the following terms have the indicated meanings:

Credibility adjustment means an adjustment to the MLR for a partially credible MCO, PIHP, or PAHP to account for a difference between the actual and target MLRs that may be due to random statistical variation.

Full credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be sufficient for the calculation of a MLR with a minimal chance that the difference between the actual and target medical loss ratio is not statistically significant. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned full credibility (or is fully credible) will not receive a credibility adjustment to its MLR.

Member months mean the number of months an enrollee or a group of enrollees is covered by an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP over a specified time period, such as a year.

MLR reporting year means a period of 12 months consistent with the rating period selected by the State.

No credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be insufficient for the calculation of a MLR. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned no credibility (or is non-credible) will not be measured against any MLR requirements.

Non-claims costs means those expenses for administrative services that are not: Incurred claims (as defined in paragraph (e)(2) of this section); expenditures on activities that improve health care quality (as defined in paragraph (e)(3) of this section); or licensing and regulatory fees, or Federal and State taxes (as defined in paragraph (f)(2) of this section).

Partial credibility means a standard for which the experience of an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP is determined to be sufficient for the calculation of a MLR but with a non-negligible chance that the difference between the actual and target medical loss ratios is statistically significant. An MCO, PIHP, or PAHP that is assigned partial credibility (or is partially credible) will receive a credibility adjustment to its MLR.

(c) MLR requirement. If a State elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs, that minimum MLR must be equal to or higher than 85 percent (the standard used for projecting actuarial soundness under § 438.4(b)) and the MLR must be calculated and reported for each MLR reporting year by the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP, consistent with this section.

(d) Calculation of the MLR. The MLR experienced for each MCO, PIHP, or PAHP in a MLR reporting year is the ratio of the numerator (as defined in paragraph (e) of this section) to the denominator (as defined in paragraph (f) of this section). A MLR may be increased by a credibility adjustment, in accordance with paragraph (h) of this section.

(e) Numerator —(1) Required elements. The numerator of an MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's MLR for a MLR reporting year is the sum of the MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's incurred claims (as defined in (e)(2) of this section); the MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's expenditures for activities that improve health care quality (as defined in paragraph (e)(3) of this section); and fraud prevention activities (as defined in paragraph (e)(4) of this section).

(2) Incurred claims. (i) Incurred claims must include the following:

(A) Direct claims that the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP paid to providers (including under capitated contracts with network providers) for services or supplies covered under the contract and services meeting the requirements of § 438.3(e) provided to enrollees.

(B) Unpaid claims liabilities for the MLR reporting year, including claims reported that are in the process of being adjusted or claims incurred but not reported.

(C) Withholds from payments made to network providers.

(D) Claims that are recoverable for anticipated coordination of benefits.

(E) Claims payments recoveries received as a result of subrogation.

(F) Incurred but not reported claims based on past experience, and modified to reflect current conditions, such as changes in exposure or claim frequency or severity.

(G) Changes in other claims-related reserves.

(H) Reserves for contingent benefits and the medical claim portion of lawsuits.

(ii) Amounts that must be deducted from incurred claims include the following:

(A) Overpayment recoveries received from network providers.

(B) Prescription drug rebates received and accrued.

(iii) Expenditures that must be included in incurred claims include the following:

(A) The amount of incentive and bonus payments made, or expected to be made, to network providers that are tied to clearly-defined, objectively measurable, and well-documented clinical or quality improvement standards that apply to providers.

(B) The amount of claims payments recovered through fraud reduction efforts, not to exceed the amount of fraud reduction expenses. The amount of fraud reduction expenses must not include activities specified in paragraph (e)(4) of this section.

(C) The amount of payments made to providers under State directed payments described in § 438.6(c).

(iv) Amounts that must either be included in or deducted from incurred claims include, respectively, net payments or receipts related to State mandated solvency funds.

(v) Amounts that must be excluded from incurred claims:

(A) Non-claims costs, as defined in paragraph (b) of this section, which include the following:

( 1 ) Amounts paid to third party vendors for secondary network savings.

( 2 ) Amounts paid to third party vendors for network development, administrative fees, claims processing, and utilization management.

( 3 ) Amounts paid, including amounts paid to a provider, for professional or administrative s

per_question.question: When does NC Medicaid pay for CAR-T cell treatment? What specific criteria have to be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid pays for CAR-T cell therapy when it is medically necessary and the policy’s specific coverage criteria are all met under current Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective April 1, 2025. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment) [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Specific criteria that must be met

NC Medicaid says CAR-T cell therapy is covered only when **all** of these are true: [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

- The CAR-T therapy has received **U.S. FDA approval**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The therapy is administered **within the FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage, [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
  - dosage and administration, [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
  - dosage forms and strengths, and [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
  - warnings and precautions. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The therapy is given at a **certified or authorized treatment center**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- If the product is subject to a **REMS** program, the treatment center must be **enrolled in the REMS**, and providers must be **trained to manage cytokine release syndrome and neurologic toxicities**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

In addition to those CAR-T-specific rules, the general Medicaid medical-necessity criteria in the policy also have to be met. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

That means the service must be:
- **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not more than the beneficiary needs; [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- able to be **safely furnished**, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- furnished in a manner **not primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The policy also says there are **no additional Medicaid-specific covered criteria** beyond those listed above. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Situations where NC Medicaid will not pay

NC Medicaid will not cover CAR-T cell therapy if the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility rules in Section 2.0, does not meet the Section 3.0 coverage criteria, the service duplicates another provider’s service, or the therapy is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

More specifically, CAR-T is not covered if any of these apply:
- the product is **not FDA-approved**; [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- it is being given **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths; [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- a product that requires **REMS** is being given at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program; [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- the beneficiary previously received **another CAR-T therapy** and this would be a **repeat treatment**; [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- the beneficiary’s **psychosocial history** limits ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- there is current beneficiary or caretaker **non-compliance** making compliance with a disciplined medical regimen improbable. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The policy separately says NC Medicaid does **not** cover a **concurrent rescue transplant with infusion of any CAR-T therapy**, because that is considered experimental. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Prior approval

NC Medicaid requires **prior approval** before CAR-T cell therapy is provided. [Policy 11A-17 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Under age 21

For Medicaid beneficiaries under 21, the policy includes the standard **EPSDT special provision**, which can allow coverage beyond ordinary policy limitations when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a condition, but EPSDT does not require coverage of services that are unsafe, ineffective, experimental, investigational, or not generally recognized as accepted medical practice. [Policy 11A-17 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: Up to what age can children on Medicaid receive fluoride varnish from their physician, and what oral screening has to accompany it?
per_question.agent_answer:
Children can receive physician-applied fluoride varnish under this policy from tooth eruption until age 3½. [Policy 1A-23 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The varnish must be part of an “oral screening package” that includes an examination, preventive oral health and dietary counseling, and application of fluoride varnish. [Policy 1A-23 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The oral screening itself must include early caries screening and detection of notable findings in the mouth using a dental mirror and directed light. [Policy 1A-23 § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The policy also requires documentation of an oral evaluation and any notable findings, preventive oral health and dietary counseling with the primary caregiver, application of fluoride varnish, and referral to a dentist if appropriate. [Policy 1A-23 § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

This policy was amended effective April 1, 2023, with a revision posted April 15, 2023. [Policy 1A-23 Change Notice 2023-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is accurate and complete. It correctly states the age limit (tooth eruption until 3½ years), accurately describes the oral screening package from §3.2.2 (examination, preventive oral health and dietary counseling, and application of fluoride varnish), and correctly details the §7.2 requirements including early caries screening, dental mirror/directed light examination, documentation requirements, and referral to dentist. All claims are supported by the Evidence blocks. The amendment date (April 1, 2023, posted April 15, 2023) is confirmed in the getAmendments evidence. Citations are precise at the section level (§3.2.2 and §7.2). No hallucinations detected.

Early caries screening and detection of notable findings (obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues) in the oral cavity using a dental mirror and directed light.

c.

an oral evaluation and any notable findings;
preventive oral health and dietary counseling with the primary caregiver;
application of fluoride varnish; and

per_question.question: An NC Innovations participant's needs cost more than their individual base budget. Can they request services beyond the budget, and what recourse do they have if they think the budget can't meet their needs?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their base budget if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the person must be told that they may request services in excess of the base budget, and that the SIS results and base budget are only guidelines, not a binding cap on what may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they must be authorized regardless of the base budget. [wrong source: Policy 8P Change Notice 2016-11-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) [wrong source: Policy 8P](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

The policy also says that when a person’s support needs are not met within the assigned base budget, Utilization Management must authorize the requested services if it determines they are medically necessary, and no formal change in the budget amount is required in order to approve services above the budget. [wrong source: Policy 8P Change Notice 2016-11-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) [wrong source: Policy 8P](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

If the participant thinks the budget cannot meet their needs, the policy gives them several forms of recourse:

- They can work with the planning team to update the Individual Support Plan (ISP) and have the Care Coordinator submit the updated ISP for Utilization Management approval.
- If a request for authorization of services is denied, the LME/MCO must notify the participant of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal.
- The participant must also be told how to file a grievance regarding the base budget if they wish to do so.

One additional limit to keep in mind is that the individual budget is not a binding funding limit, but the waiver as a whole generally has a $135,000 cost limit unless the policy’s stated exception criteria are met.

So the short answer is: the base budget is a guideline, not an absolute cap, and the participant can ask for medically necessary services above it. If the system refuses, the participant can pursue an appeal of the denied service request and can also file a grievance about the base budget.

The policy text I relied on is from Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, which shows an amended date of April 1, 2023, and I also confirmed that the document has amendment history, with the latest surfaced authoritative amendment record in the corpus identified as the 2016-11-01 revision notice.

Title: Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes
Policy: 8P
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched category.
Content:
A Level is assigned every person on the NC Innovations Waiver. This level is based on the Support Intensity Scale ('SIS') which is the assessment instrument used to measure individual support needs.
The SIS scores are uploaded to SIS On-line with AAIDD.  Within 15 calendar days of receiving notice that the SIS has been uploaded, NC Medicaid, or their designee, applies the algorithm and assigns an initial level and individual budget.  If a SIS is updated, the results of the SIS may indicate a change in the level of support needs.  This may result in a new Individual Budget Tool Level and base budget being assigned. Within thirty (30) calendar days of a SIS being performed and NC Medicaid, or their designee's notification, NC Medicaid, or their designee will determine if there has been a Level change and the LME/MCO will notify the beneficiary in writing within 15 days of receiving notice from NC Medicaid, or their designee.  The beneficiary will also be notified if there is not a Level change.  A Level change may not always result in a change in the beneficiary's base budget, but the beneficiary will always be notified if there is a Level change and budget change.
If the beneficiary's level change has resulted in an increase in budget, that budget increase can take effect sixty (60) calendar days from the date on the letter. During that sixty (60) calendar day period, the individual can develop an update to his/her Individual Support Plan ('ISP') with the planning team allowing for the increased services, if they choose. The Care Coordinator will submit an updated ISP to UM for approval. If the beneficiary's Level change has resulted in a decrease in budget, the budget decrease will take effect at the end of the individual's most recently approved Annual ISP. No currently authorized services will be reduced as a result of the budget change. The letters notifying the individual of the decrease in budget will notify the individual of the following:
He or she may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget; and
The results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized, and if the LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.
If any request for authorization of services is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal
How to file a grievance regarding the base budget if he or she wishes to do so.

Content:
The Individual Budget is only one measure of a beneficiary's likely current needs and is not a binding limit on the amount of funding for any period of time. The Individual Budget is reviewed no less frequently than annually by the PIHP. The Individual Budget includes only Base Budget Services. NonBase Budget services are not included. Base Budget services are the core habilitation and support services in the waiver. Non-Base Budget services are preventative services, and equipment. Combined these services may not total more than the $135,000 cost limit within the waiver unless the follow criteria is met:
An individual may exceed the $135,000 waiver limit, to ensure health, safety and wellbeing, if the following criteria is met:
Beneficiaries utilizing Supported Living Level III:
lives independently without his or her family in a home that s/he owns, rents or leases, and
receives Supported Living Level III, and
requires 24 hour support.

Content:
Medicaid
Clinical Coverage Policy No: 8-P
Amended Date: April 1, 2023
Monitoring takes place in all service settings and on a schedule outlined in the ISP.
The Care Coordinator is responsible for monitoring the ISP, and reviews goals at a minimum frequency based on the target date assigned to each goal. Goals may be, and often are, reviewed more frequently, based on the needs of the beneficiary.  The Care Coordinator also maintains close contact with the beneficiary, the legally responsible person or parent or guardian (if applicable), providers, and other members of the person-centered planning team, noting any recommended revisions needed.  This ensures that changes are noted, and updates are effectuated in a timely manner.
Monitoring methods also consist of contacts (face-to-face and telephone calls) with other members of the ISP team and review of service documentation. A standard monitoring checklist is used to ensure that the following issues are monitored:
Verification that services are provided as outlined in the ISP;
The beneficiary has access to services;
Identification of any problems that may arise;
The services meet the needs of the beneficiary;
The back-up staffing plans are documented;
Issues of health and welfare (rights restrictions, medical care, abuse, neglect or exploitation, behavior support plan) are addressed;
That the beneficiary has been offered a free choice of providers; and
That non-waiver services needs have been addressed.
Care Coordinator monitoring occurs monthly and consists of the following:
A beneficiary that is new to the waiver receives face-to-face visits for the first six months and then on a schedule agreed to by the ISP team thereafter, no less than quarterly, to meet their health and safety needs;
A beneficiary whose services are provided by guardians and relatives living in the home of the beneficiary receives monthly face-to-face monitoring visits;
A beneficiary who lives in residential programs receives face-to-face monitoring visits monthly;
A beneficiary who chooses the individual family-directed service option receives face-to-face monitoring visits monthly;
For the months that the beneficiary does not receive face-to-face monitoring, the Care Coordinator has telephone contact with the beneficiary to ensure that there are no issues that need to be addressed;
At least one service is utilized monthly, per waiver eligibility requirements;
NC Innovations services utilized do not exceed authorization.  If there is an emergency, the Care Coordinator shall ensure that beneficiary's needs are met and ensure that any updates to the LOC and ISP, based upon the changes in needs of the beneficiary, are processed in a timely manner; and
Home and Community Based Services (HCBS) rules are met. Any concerns noted by the Care Coordinator regarding HCBS (such as privacy, restriction
of rights, access to food) must be reported to the PIHP. Any restrictions to HCBS must be addressed in the ISP.

Content:
Clinical Coverage Policy No: 8-P
Amended Date: April 1, 2023
All Requests for Community Living and Supports require prior approval by the PIHP:
Requests for up to 12 hours daily may be authorized for the entire plan year.
Requests for up to 16 hours daily may be authorized for a six-month timeframe, within the plan year.
Requests for more than 16 hours daily are authorized for up to a 90-day period within the plan year. In situations requiring an authorization beyond the initial 90-day period, the PIHP shall approve such authorization based on review of Medical Necessity. The treatment team should meet to review individuals' status and identify sustainable supports, if available and information from the meeting should be included in the individual's ISP.  Review of other options should include options within the Innovations Waiver, as well as options outside of the Innovations waiver such as Medicaid State Plan Services.
The service may be provided in the home or community. The involvement of unpaid supports in the generalization of the service is an important aspect to ensure that achieved goals are practiced and maintained.  Services may be allowed in the private home of the provider or staff of an Employer of Record at the discretion and agreement of the support team and when consistent with the ISP goals. If services are provided in the primary residence of the provider or staff of the employer of record, the Health and Safety Checklist must be completed before service begins and every six months thereafter.

per_question.question: What does it take to become a certified HIV case management provider for NC Medicaid, and what circumstances can lead to a provider losing that certification?
per_question.agent_answer:
To become a certified HIV case management provider for NC Medicaid, an agency must first obtain certification from NC Medicaid or its designated contractor before it can be considered for Medicaid enrollment as an HIV Case Management provider. Eligible agency types may include home health agencies, home care agencies, hospices, health departments, hospitals, departments of social services, federally qualified health clinics, rural health clinics, community-based organizations, and local management entities.

## What it takes to become certified

An agency must have a documented successful record of three years providing or managing HIV Case Management programs.

The agency must ensure its HIV case managers meet the policy’s qualification, experience, and competency standards, and its supervisors must also meet the required supervisory qualifications and case-management experience standards. [unverified: The agency must ensure its HIV case managers meet the policy’s qualification, experience, and competency standards, and its supervisors must also meet the required supervisory qualifications and case-management experience standards.]

For case managers specifically, the policy allows several education/credential pathways, but all case managers must also have two years’ case-management experience and must possess or acquire, through cross-training, a clinical understanding of HIV documented in their personnel file.

Supervisors must meet one of the listed education/licensure pathways and also have three years’ case-management experience.

Case managers must be able to perform intake, assessment, reassessment, care planning, coordination, conferencing, implementation, referral and linkage, crisis intervention, monitoring and follow-up, and discharge or termination functions.

Case managers must also demonstrate specific HIV knowledge and practice skills, including basic knowledge of HIV disease, prevention, treatment techniques, communication, documentation, cultural sensitivity, and ability to assess needs and resources. The policy requires documented proof of the basic HIV knowledge within one year of hire.

All HIV case managers and supervisors must complete North Carolina state-sponsored basic training within 90 days of employment, and that training must be completed before any case management units are billed.

All HIV case managers and supervisors must also complete 12 hours of continuing education related to HIV Case Management each year, with 6 of those hours being clinically oriented training.

Each physical site must be enrolled with NC Medicaid as an HIV Case Management provider, and the agency must comply with applicable state and federal Medicaid participation laws, maintain certification, comply with certification and monitoring processes, maintain a quality improvement plan, allow review of records and operations, and report proposed and actual business changes within the policy timeframes.

Within one year of Medicaid enrollment as a provider, the agency must achieve national accreditation from at least one designated accrediting body listed in the policy.

To obtain initial certification, the provider must submit a complete and signed application including the administrative, case-management, and human-resource information required by the policy, and the initial certification is valid for one year.

The recertification materials show what NC Medicaid expects agencies to maintain and document. [unverified: The recertification materials show what NC Medicaid expects agencies to maintain and document.]
The recertification application requires listing all current case managers and supervisors with hire dates, the counties served, and the services the agency provides.

The recertification application and checklist also require agencies to maintain or submit policies and supporting documents such as confidentiality, beneficiary grievance rights, nondiscrimination, code of ethics, conflict of interest, electronic records, medical-record retention, freedom of choice, transfer/discharge, abuse/neglect/exploitation policies, a quality assurance policy, chart review results, organizational chart, community resources, ownership information, staff credentials, networking plan with CCNC or the PCP, and HR policies, procedures, or plans.

The application also requires the agency to agree that Medicaid may review beneficiary records and other HIV case-management information, that the provider will verify staff qualifications and credentials, provide regular qualified supervision, maintain a business plan and computer capabilities, and comply with applicable laws including HIPAA and record-retention requirements.

A newly certified provider receives two quality-assurance site visits within the first year after certification, and those visits review staff qualifications and training, case-management services, documentation, billing comparisons, complaints, and quality-improvement activities.

## When a provider can lose certification

A provider can be denied certification up front if it has previously been decertified as an HIV Case Management provider, if its provider number has been suspended because of Program Integrity sanctions, or if it has failed to repay money owed to the North Carolina Medicaid program.

A certified provider may be decertified if any listed ground is substantiated, and the policy says the list is not all-inclusive.

The listed grounds for decertification include failure to provide core service components, fraudulent billing practices, an owner being convicted of a felony, falsification of records, violation of beneficiary confidentiality, and employing staff who do not meet the policy’s qualification criteria.

Other listed grounds include failure to complete a written plan of correction within 30 calendar days when required, failure of staff to complete mandatory basic training within 90 days, failure of staff to obtain required continuing education, failure to provide adequate supervision, failure to submit required documentation on time, failure to maintain documentation sufficient to support billing, and failure to implement and enforce a quality-improvement program.

A provider may also be decertified for failing to notify NC Medicaid or its designated contractor of agency changes within the required timelines, failing to comply with applicable federal and state laws and Medicaid rules, failing to enroll any beneficiaries within four months of certification, or failing to achieve or maintain the certification requirements in Section 6.2.

Quality-assurance visits can trigger provisional recertification, decertification, or referral to Program Integrity if the provider fails to adhere to policy requirements. If unmet program requirements are found during a site visit, the provider must submit a written plan of correction within 30 calendar days when requested.

For recertification specifically, the provider must submit a complete signed recertification application within 60 calendar days of receipt, provide changed items from the initial certification package, provide all HIV case-manager and supervisor credentials, submit annual quality-improvement summaries with outcome metrics, and submit to an on-site recertification visit. Applications still not meeting criteria after 90 days are returned as incomplete and no further action shall be required by NC Medicaid or the DHHS designated contractor.

If NC Medicaid or its designated agent notifies a Medicaid-enrolled provider that it is no longer certified to provide HIV Case Management services, the provider may request a reconsideration review under 10A NCAC 22F.0402.

uncited_claims: Eligible agency types may include home health agencies, home care agencies, hospices, health departments, hospitals, departments of social services, federally qualified health clinics, rural health clinics, community-based organizations, and local management entities.

[unverified: The agency must ensure its HIV case managers meet the policy’s qualification, experience, and competency standards, and its supervisors must also meet the required supervisory qualifications and case-management experience standards.]

For case managers specifically, the policy allows several education/credential pathways, but all case managers must also have two years’ case-management experience and must possess or acquire, through cross-training, a clinical understanding of HIV documented in their personnel file.
The policy requires documented proof of the basic HIV knowledge within one year of hire.

All HIV case managers and supervisors must complete North Carolina state-sponsored basic training within 90 days of employment, and that training must be completed before any case management units are billed.
All HIV case managers and supervisors must also complete 12 hours of continuing education related to HIV Case Management each year, with 6 of those hours being clinically oriented training.

Each physical site must be enrolled with NC Medicaid as an HIV Case Management provider, and the agency must comply with applicable state and federal Medicaid participation laws, maintain certification, comply with certification and monitoring processes, maintain a quality improvement plan, allow review of records and operations, and report proposed and actual business changes within the policy timeframes.

A newly certified provider receives two quality-assurance site visits within the first year after certification, and those visits review staff qualifications and training, case-management services, documentation, billing comparisons, complaints, and quality-improvement activities.
A certified provider may be decertified if any listed ground is substantiated, and the policy says the list is not all-inclusive.

The listed grounds for decertification include failure to provide core service components, fraudulent billing practices, an owner being convicted of a felony, falsification of records, violation of beneficiary confidentiality, and employing staff who do not meet the policy’s qualification criteria.

Other listed grounds include failure to complete a written plan of correction within 30 calendar days when required, failure of staff to complete mandatory basic training within 90 days, failure of staff to obtain required continuing education, failure to provide adequate supervision, failure to submit required documentation on time, failure to maintain documentation sufficient to support billing, and failure to implement and enforce a quality-improvement program.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s257
Title: Approving extraordinary circumstances
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
The CAP/DA case manager is responsible for reviewing supporting documentation to determine the eligibility of a legally responsible person to become the paid caregiver. The CAP/DA case manager uses supporting documentation to make decisions that align with one of the five extraordinary circumstances. Required supporting documentation are listed below.
Physician's orders
Personnel actions forms (PAF)
Medical documentation outlining the beneficiary's need for short term isolation, physician
Rejection correspondence from In-home care agencies ordered 24-hour direct observation, and special health needs
When an individual meets the extraordinary circumstances described above, the maximum number of hours that can be approved for payment for providing personal care services is up to 40 hours per week. The approved hours are based primarily on the assessed needs identified in the assessment.
The payment for instrumental activities of daily living such as meal preparation, laundry, money management, home maintenance, shopping, and medication management is inclusive with the payment for the performance or assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) tasks.
When the legal guardian is authorized to receive payment for providing personal assistance services, the CAP/DA beneficiary monitored closely by the case management entity (CME) to ensure quality assurance of the health, safety and well-being of the CAP/DA beneficiary and provides the controls to ensure that payments are made only for the services authorized to provide. The assigned CME shall perform a bi-monthly (two times per month) monitoring visits, one in-person and the second telephonically, to ensure the services are provided according to the service plan and the CAP/DA participation business requirements.
A legally responsible person shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment because of an unjustified unwillingness to work with Home Care Agencies/In-Home Aide Agencies. A legally responsible person shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment if there are other providers available to render personal care services when the CAP/DA beneficiary has been discharged from a Home Care Agency or In-Home Aide Agency due to non-complaint or violent behavior exhibited by the CAP/DA beneficiary or the legal guardian.
A legal guardian who is currently approved to receive payment for performing personal care services to a CAP/DA beneficiary has previously met the conditions outlined above; therefore, a grandfathering process is not necessary.
When a determination is made in the best interest of the CAP/DA beneficiary to have a legally responsible person to provide personal care services, a physician's recommendation must be provided to the case manager outlining the specific care needs of the CAP/DA beneficiary and how those needs can only be provided by the legally responsible person. In collaboration with the physician's recommendation, an analysis of the case record is performed to evaluate the legally responsible person's compliance with treatment and service plans and to ensure critical incident reports did not implicate the legally responsible person to be negligent. The physical health of the legally responsible person is considered and evaluated to ensure the health and well-being of the beneficiary. No more than a total of 40 hours per week may be authorized and approved.
42 CFR §440.167 prohibits federal financial participation (FFP) for payments to legally responsible individuals for the provision of State plan personal care services or similar services. This prohibition is based on the presumption that legally responsible individuals may not be paid for support that they are ordinarily obligated to provide. Legally responsible individuals do not include the parent of an adult beneficiary (including a parent who also may be a legal guardian) or other types of relatives, except as provided by state law).

Content:
The CAP/DA case manager is responsible for reviewing supporting documentation to determine the eligibility of a legally responsible person to become the paid caregiver. The CAP/DA case manager uses supporting documentation to make decisions that align with one of the five extraordinary circumstances. Required supporting documentation are listed below.
Physician's orders
Personnel actions forms (PAF)
Rejection correspondence from In-home care agencies
Medical documentation outlining the beneficiary's need for short term isolation, physician ordered 24-hour direct observation, and special health needs.
The payment for instrumental activities of daily living such as meal preparation, laundry, money management, home maintenance, shopping, and medication management is inclusive with the payment for the performance or assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) tasks.
When the legal guardian is authorized to receive payment for providing personal assistance services, the CAP/DA beneficiary is enrolled in the coordinated caregiving waiver service. Enrollment in this service shall provide quality assurance of the health, safety and well-being of the CAP/DA beneficiary and provides the controls to ensure that payments are made only for the services authorized to provide.
The assigned Case Management Entity (CME) shall monitor the CAP/DA beneficiary closely to ensure the services are provided according to the service plan and the waiver participation business requirements.
A legal guardian shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment because of an unjustified unwillingness to work with Home Health Agencies/In-Home Aide Agencies. A legal guardian shall not be approved to provide personal care services and receive payment if there are other providers available to render personal care services when the waiver participant has been discharged from a Home Health Agency/In-Home Aide Agency due to non-complaint or violent behavior exhibited by the waiver participant or the legal guardian.
A legal guardian who is currently approved to receive payment for performing personal care services to a CAP/DA beneficiary has previously met the conditions outlined above; therefore, a grandfathering process is not necessary.
When it is determined to be in the best interest of the CAP/DA beneficiary to have a legally responsible individual to provide personal care services, a physician's recommendation must be provided to the case manager outlining the specific care needs of the CAP/DA beneficiary and how those needs can only be provided by the legally responsible individual. In conjunction with the physician's recommendation, an analysis of the case record is performed to evaluate the legally responsible individual's compliance with treatment orders and service plans, and critical incident report conclusions did not implicate the legally responsible individual to be negligent. In addition, the physical health of the legally responsible individual is a contributing component to ensure the ongoing health and safety of the CAP/DA beneficiary.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:12B:6.1.5
Title: 6.1.5 Case Management Supervisor's Experience
Section: 6.1.5
Policy: 12B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
Case management experience must encompass the functions of intake, assessment, reassessment, care planning, case coordination, case conferencing, care plan implementation, referral, linkage and resource development, crisis intervention, monitoring and follow -up of services provided and discharge or termination.
Knowledge, Skills and Abilities
In addition to those listed for the CM, the case management supervisor must possess and demonstrate the following knowledge, skills and abilities:
Ability to direct and evaluate the scope and quality of case management services;
Knowledgeable in case management principals, procedures and practices;
Ability to conduct detailed analytical evaluations and studies, and prepare related reports and recommendations; and
Apply professional level of knowledge of federal and state assistance programs for HIV positive population.
The provider shall identify the HIV CM program supervisor within the organization. The supervisor is to provide supervision that addresses both the clinical and professional aspects of the CM's job performance. This is defined as providing regularly scheduled assistance by a qualified professional to a staff member who is working directly with beneficiaries.
The purpose of clinical supervision is to ensure that each beneficiary receives case management services which are consistent with accepted standards of practice and the needs of the beneficiary and care plan.
Documentation of supervisory review of CM's caseload and proper utilization of case management services is required. The supervisor shall attest to the accuracy of the documentation by a personal signature to include credentials and title. Each beneficiary record must reflect supervisory review every 4 weeks at a minimum. The frequency of the reviews must be increased if the findings warrant such action. The review must include the following: the beneficiary record to assure that all required paperwork as defined by this policy is in the record and progress notes must be reviewed for compliance with the requirements in Subsections 7.5 and 7.6. The billing must be checked for accuracy to assure it corresponds to the progress notes. This is not billable case management time.
